sentence: The sources are fragmentary. There may be no evidence for the alleged agreement; whatever evidence exists is slight. The account offers ___.

taskText: The sources are fragmentary. There may be no evidence for the alleged agreement; whatever evidence exists is slight. The account offers ___.
text: Choose the cautious wording that preserves both a very small upper estimate and uncertainty about whether any evidence exists. The sources are fragmentary. There may be no evidence for the alleged agreement; whatever evidence exists is slight. The account offers ___.
options: a little evidence
no evidence whatsoever
some evidence, if not much
little, if any, evidence
answer: little, if any, evidence
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1181:Calibrating little if any against existence claims
explanation: Little limits the amount, while if any explicitly keeps zero evidence possible.

rationales.a little evidence: A little positively presents some evidence as existing, which the source assessment leaves uncertain.
rationales.no evidence whatsoever: This resolves the uncertainty as zero, making a stronger claim than the sources permit.
rationales.little, if any, evidence: Little limits the amount, while if any explicitly keeps zero evidence possible.
rationales.some evidence, if not much: Some evidence asserts a positive amount; if not much qualifies quantity without withdrawing that existence claim.

sentence: Every site was inspected by at least one engineer, but there was no engineer who inspected all the sites.
setupText: Choose the sentence that states both coverage conditions explicitly.
taskText: Every site was inspected by at least one engineer, but there was no engineer who inspected all the sites.
text: Choose the sentence that states both coverage conditions explicitly. Every site was inspected by at least one engineer, but there was no engineer who inspected all the sites.
options: An engineer inspected every site, but not all engineers inspected a site.
Each site had an engineer inspect it, but no engineer inspected every site.
No engineer inspected any site, although each site was assigned an engineer.
Every engineer inspected a site, but some sites were not inspected.
answer: Each site had an engineer inspect it, but no engineer inspected every site.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1182:Distributing existential coverage without a universal individual
explanation: Each site secures complete site coverage; no engineer...every site excludes a single engineer with complete coverage.

rationales.An engineer inspected every site, but no: This introduces one engineer who covered all sites, contradicting the second condition.
rationales.Each site had an engineer inspect it, bu: Each site secures complete site coverage; no engineer...every site excludes a single engineer with complete coverage.
rationales.No engineer inspected any site, although: Assignment is not inspection, and denying all inspections contradicts the first condition.
rationales.Every engineer inspected a site, but som: This quantifies over engineers instead of ensuring site coverage, and explicitly leaves sites uninspected.

sentence: None of the reviewers accepted all of the report's assumptions.

answer: Every reviewer rejected or withheld acceptance of at least one assumption.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1183:Negated complete acceptance with varying exceptions
explanation: For each reviewer, at least one assumption was outside the accepted set; the sentence need not identify a shared exception.

rationales.Every reviewer rejected every assumption: None accepted all rules out complete acceptance, not partial acceptance.
rationales.There is one particular assumption that: Different reviewers may have withheld acceptance from different assumptions.
rationales.Some reviewers accepted every assumption: None of the reviewers excludes any reviewer who accepted the full set.
rationales.Every reviewer rejected or withheld acce: For each reviewer, at least one assumption was outside the accepted set; the sentence need not identify a shared exception.

focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1184:Editing near-universal coverage with a restricted subject and indefinite object
explanation: Nearly every preserves almost all; surviving still restricts the letters, and a supplier preserves the per-letter existence claim.

rationales.Nearly every surviving letter mentions a: Nearly every preserves almost all; surviving still restricts the letters, and a supplier preserves the per-letter existence claim.
rationales.Nearly every supplier appears in a survi: This quantifies the suppliers instead of the letters, asserting broad supplier coverage that the original does not establish.

sentence: Original: 'Every witness recognized someone in the photograph.' Proposed summary: 'There was one person in the photograph whom every witness recognized.'
setupText: Choose the accurate assessment of the proposed edit.
taskText: Original: 'Every witness recognized someone in the photograph.' Proposed summary: 'There was one person in the photograph whom every witness recognized.'
text: Choose the accurate assessment of the proposed edit. Original: 'Every witness recognized someone in the photograph.' Proposed summary: 'There was one person in the photograph whom every witness recognized.'
options: The summary is equivalent; its opening merely makes the recognized person easier to refer to.
The summary weakens every to one and no longer includes all the witnesses.
The summary adds a shared recognized person; the original allows witnesses to recognize different people.
The summary contradicts the original, which requires a different person for each witness.
answer: The summary adds a shared recognized person; the original allows witnesses to recognize different people.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1185:Detecting a shared existential referent added to a recognition report
explanation: One witness could recognize only Ana and another only Bo. Each would recognize someone, but no person would be recognized by both, so the summary is not guaranteed.

rationales.The summary is equivalent; its opening m: The new opening fixes a single person as recognized by everyone. The original can be true when witnesses recognize different people.
rationales.The summary weakens every to one and no: One counts the recognized person, not the witnesses; every witness still includes the full witness group.
rationales.The summary adds a shared recognized per: One witness could recognize only Ana and another only Bo. Each would recognize someone, but no person would be recognized by both, so the summary is not guaranteed.
rationales.The summary contradicts the original, wh: The original allows different recognized people but does not require them; it also permits everyone to recognize the same person.

sentence: All but one of the panelists declined to endorse the recommendation.

focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1186:Exception scope without inferring a positive or undecided stance
explanation: All but one creates a single exception to declining, without telling us whether that person endorsed, deferred or withheld a response.

rationales.Only one panelist endorsed it; the other: Not declining is not itself endorsement: the exceptional panelist might still be undecided.
rationales.Only one panelist did not decline; their: All but one creates a single exception to declining, without telling us whether that person endorsed, deferred or withheld a response.
rationales.One panelist declined; the others did no: This makes one the size of the declining group instead of the exception to that group.
rationales.One panelist has yet to decide; the othe: Indecision is possible for the exception, but the original does not specifically establish it.

sentence: Journal A says, 'Few of our fifty submissions were accepted.' Journal B says, 'Few of our five thousand submissions were accepted.'
setupText: Choose the defensible comparison. Both journals use 'few' for a low proportion of their own submissions.
taskText: Journal A says, 'Few of our fifty submissions were accepted.' Journal B says, 'Few of our five thousand submissions were accepted.'
text: Choose the defensible comparison. Both journals use 'few' for a low proportion of their own submissions. Journal A says, 'Few of our fifty submissions were accepted.' Journal B says, 'Few of our five thousand submissions were accepted.'
options: The journals accepted the same number because both used few.
B must have accepted more manuscripts because it received more.
Each journal accepted at most four manuscripts.
B may have accepted more manuscripts than A, despite both using few.
answer: B may have accepted more manuscripts than A, despite both using few.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1187:Context-dependent proportional few across unequal populations
explanation: A low proportion of a large pool can exceed a low proportion of a small pool in absolute count; 'few' alone does not settle the comparison.

rationales.The journals accepted the same number be: 'Few' is context-dependent; using the same vague quantifier does not establish equal counts across different-sized groups.
rationales.B must have accepted more manuscripts be: A larger submission pool does not guarantee a larger accepted count without actual acceptance figures.
rationales.Each journal accepted at most four manus: 'Few' does not have a fixed ceiling of four, especially when it describes a proportion of thousands.
rationales.B may have accepted more manuscripts tha: A low proportion of a large pool can exceed a low proportion of a small pool in absolute count; 'few' alone does not settle the comparison.

explanation: A considerable number makes not a few direct, while keeping that quantity inside the claim made separately about each report.

rationales.Each report leaves a considerable number: A considerable number makes not a few direct, while keeping that quantity inside the claim made separately about each report.

rationales.Some reports leave a considerable number: Some reports weakens the original each report, so it no longer covers every report individually.

sentence: A discrepancy affecting the final total must be investigated. If ___ is discovered, record it separately.

focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1190:Anaphoric such under conditional any

The summary wrongly changes rejection of a shared pair into rejection of separate pairs.

The summary changes an approximate total into an exact total.
answer: The summary assumes that the reviewers' pairs did not overlap.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1192:Diagnosing unsupported cross-person distinctness in a summary
explanation: Different separates the two proposals within each reviewer's pair. It does not establish that one reviewer's pair differs from another's.

rationales.The summary assumes that the reviewers': Different separates the two proposals within each reviewer's pair. It does not establish that one reviewer's pair differs from another's.
rationales.The summary incorrectly assumes that eac: Two different proposals explicitly gives each reviewer more than one rejection, so that inference is licensed.

rationales.The summary changes an approximate total: The original provides exact per-reviewer counts, not an approximate total of distinct proposals; overlap is the missing information.

setupText: Choose the accurate assessment of the change from 'any' to 'only'.
taskText: Original: 'Any account supported by two independent sources will be included.' Edit: 'Only accounts supported by two independent sources will be included.'
text: Choose the accurate assessment of the change from 'any' to 'only'. Original: 'Any account supported by two independent sources will be included.' Edit: 'Only accounts supported by two independent sources will be included.'
options: The original guarantees inclusion for qualifying accounts; the edit excludes others without guaranteeing inclusion for the qualifying accounts.
Both versions guarantee inclusion for qualifying accounts; the edit merely expresses the same rule more directly.
The original excludes nonqualifying accounts; the edit guarantees inclusion whenever the source condition is met.
Neither version commits to including qualifying accounts; both merely express a preference for independently supported sources.
answer: The original guarantees inclusion for qualifying accounts; the edit excludes others without guaranteeing inclusion for the qualifying accounts.
focusKey: coverage-determiners-and-quantifiers-c2-1193:Any versus only in sufficient and necessary inclusion conditions
explanation: 'Any...will' gives a sufficient condition for inclusion. 'Only' makes that condition necessary, without preserving the guarantee for every qualifying account.

rationales.Both versions guarantee inclusion for qu: 'Only' restricts what may be included, but does not guarantee inclusion of every account meeting that restriction.
rationales.The original excludes nonqualifying acco: This reverses the functions: 'any' guarantees inclusion on qualification, while 'only' makes qualification necessary.
rationales.The original guarantees inclusion for qu: 'Any...will' gives a sufficient condition for inclusion. 'Only' makes that condition necessary, without preserving the guarantee for every qualifying account.
rationales.Neither version commits to including qua: 'Will be included' in the original is a commitment, and 'only' in the edit is a restriction, not a preference.

explanation: No applicant places every member of the class outside the permitted group, stating the blanket prohibition clearly.

explanation: Tested to date remains a restriction on the solutions, and have failed preserves an outcome claim rather than a claim of impossibility.

rationales.Every solution has failed each test cond: This adds a solution-by-test universal and removes the restriction to tested solutions.

rationales.All the solutions tested to date have fa: Tested to date remains a restriction on the solutions, and have failed preserves an outcome claim rather than a claim of impossibility.
